title: Doses in units: insulin U100, heparin, enoxaparin and nystatin
blurb: Handle doses written in units: convert units to mL from the label, and keep units and mL apart.
question: A person is prescribed insulin 18 units. The vial label reads 100 units in 1 mL. What volume in mL contains the dose?

teach.h: Units are an amount, not a volume
teach.body: Formal rule: a unit measures biological activity, so the label gives units per mL and volume = (units prescribed ÷ units in stock) × stock volume. Plain English: treat "units" exactly like mg in the want ÷ have sum. Insulin, heparin, oxytocin and nystatin are prescribed in units. The word "units" is written in full on charts, never U or IU. Insulin and heparin are stretch items on Part A; midwifery papers use units for oxytocin and nystatin.
teach.cite: Pearson VUE NMC practice papers; FACTS sheet section 3

teach.h: Worked example: Mrs Kowalski on a surgical ward
teach.body: Ewa Kowalski, 67, is prescribed heparin 7,500 units subcutaneously. The ampoule says 25,000 units in 1 mL. Volume = 7,500 ÷ 25,000 × 1 = 0.3 mL. Sense-check: 7,500 is under a third of 25,000, so the volume is under a third of 1 mL. Type 0.3 mL.

teach.caption: Insulin is given with an insulin syringe or pen marked in units; Part A may ask for the mL equivalent.

teach.text: Units and mL are not the same thing. 18 units of U100 insulin is 0.18 mL, not 18 mL. Insulin is always measured in an insulin syringe or pen, never a general-purpose syringe. In the answer box, check whether the stem asks for units or for mL.

teach.h: Prefilled syringes: multiply by their volume
teach.body: Enoxaparin and dalteparin come in prefilled syringes such as 80 mg in 0.8 mL or 10,000 units in 0.4 mL. The stock volume is not 1 mL, so finish with × 0.8 or × 0.4. 60 mg from 80 mg in 0.8 mL = 60 ÷ 80 × 0.8 = 0.6 mL. Forgetting that step is the commonest error.

items: Units work exactly like mg in want ÷ have × volume.
U100 insulin: 100 units in 1 mL, so 18 units = 0.18 mL.
Never treat units as mL: that is a hundredfold or greater error.
Prefilled syringes: multiply by the syringe volume (0.4 or 0.8 mL).
Type unit answers as a number only when the box prints "units".

summary: You can now calculate volumes and doses for medicines prescribed in units, including insulin, heparin, enoxaparin and nystatin. You can also keep units and mL apart and handle prefilled syringes that are not 1 mL.

A.q: A person is prescribed insulin 18 units. The vial label reads insulin 100 units in 1 mL. What volume in mL contains the dose? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
A.why: Want ÷ have × volume = 18 ÷ 100 × 1 = 0.18 mL. On an insulin syringe this is the 18 unit mark.

whyNot.0: This treats units as mL: 18 units is not 18 mL.
whyNot.1: This uses 10 units in 1 mL, a tenfold error.
whyNot.3: This is have ÷ want, the inverted fraction.

A.q: A patient is prescribed heparin 7,500 units by subcutaneous injection. The ampoule label reads heparin 25,000 units in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.1: This is have ÷ want, the inverted fraction.
whyNot.2: This uses a 5,000 units in 1 mL strength, not the 25,000 on the label.
whyNot.3: This adds a zero to 7,500, a tenfold error.

A.q: A baby is prescribed nystatin oral suspension 100,000 units four times a day. The label reads 100,000 units in 1 mL. What total volume is given in 24 hours? Please use the correct unit.
A.why: Each dose = 100,000 ÷ 100,000 × 1 = 1 mL. Four doses in 24 hours = 4 × 1 = 4 mL.

whyNot.0: This is the volume for one dose, not the four doses given in 24 hours.
whyNot.1: This uses 10,000 units in 1 mL, a tenfold error.
whyNot.2: This uses 1,000,000 units in 1 mL, a tenfold error the other way.

B.q: A man is prescribed enoxaparin 60 mg by subcutaneous injection. The prefilled syringe label reads 80 mg in 0.8 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
B.why: Want ÷ have × volume = 60 ÷ 80 × 0.8 = 0.6 mL. Sense-check: the strength is 100 mg per mL, so 60 mg is 0.6 mL.

whyNot.0: This forgets to multiply by the 0.8 mL syringe volume (0.75 rounds to 0.8).
whyNot.2: This is have ÷ want, the inverted fraction.
whyNot.3: This uses 10 mg per mL, a tenfold error.

B.q: A U100 insulin syringe holds insulin 100 units in 1 mL. How many units of insulin are in 0.25 mL?

whyNot.0: This uses 10 units per mL, a tenfold error.
whyNot.1: This uses 1,000 units per mL, a tenfold error the other way.

B.q: A woman weighing 72 kg is prescribed enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg by subcutaneous injection. The prefilled syringe label reads 120 mg in 0.8 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.1: This forgets to multiply by the 0.8 mL syringe volume.
whyNot.2: This is have ÷ want, the inverted fraction.
whyNot.3: This assumes 100 mg per mL; this syringe is 150 mg per mL.

C.q: A man weighing 80 kg is prescribed heparin 75 units/kg by intravenous injection. The ampoule label reads heparin 5,000 units in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: This is have ÷ want, the inverted fraction (0.83 rounds to 0.8).
whyNot.1: This uses a 1,000 units in 1 mL strength, not the 5,000 on the label.
whyNot.3: This uses 500 units per mL, a tenfold error.

C.q: An insulin pen cartridge contains 300 units in 3 mL. A person injects 24 units each time. How many complete 24 unit doses does one full cartridge give?
C.why: 300 ÷ 24 = 12.5, so the cartridge gives 12 doses of 24 units; the half dose left over is not a complete dose.

whyNot.0: This rounds 12.5 up, but the 13th dose would be only half.
whyNot.2: This is the exact quotient; part of a dose is not a dose.
whyNot.3: This misreads 24 units as 2.4, a tenfold error.

C.q: A person is prescribed dalteparin 5,000 units by subcutaneous injection. The prefilled syringe label reads 10,000 units in 0.4 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: This forgets to multiply by the 0.4 mL syringe volume.
whyNot.1: This is have ÷ want, the inverted fraction.
whyNot.2: This uses 1,000 units in the syringe, a tenfold error.

reteach.title: Units in, mL out
reteach.question: Heparin 5,000 units is prescribed. The label reads 25,000 units in 1 mL. What volume?

blocks.body: 5,000 ÷ 25,000 × 1 = 0.2 mL. The word "units" sits where "mg" usually does; nothing else changes.

blocks.text: Reading a dose in units as a volume in mL. 5,000 units of heparin is a fraction of a millilitre, not 5 mL or 5,000 mL.

explain.h: U100 means 100 units in each mL
explain.body: To change insulin units to mL, divide by 100. 8 units = 8 ÷ 100 = 0.08 mL.

test.q: A person is prescribed insulin 8 units. The vial label reads insulin 100 units in 1 mL. What volume in mL contains the dose? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.2: This uses 10 units in 1 mL, a tenfold error.
whyNot.3: This is have ÷ want, the inverted fraction.

test.q: A patient is prescribed heparin 5,000 units by subcutaneous injection. The ampoule label reads heparin 25,000 units in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: This is have ÷ want, the inverted fraction.
whyNot.2: This adds a zero to the dose, a tenfold error.
whyNot.3: This uses 10,000 units in 1 mL, not the 25,000 on the label.

explain.h: mg to units when the stem links them
explain.body: Enoxaparin labels may state 1 mg = 100 units. Multiply the mg by 100: 40 mg = 4,000 units.

test.q: A patient is prescribed enoxaparin 40 mg. The label states 1 mg = 100 units. How many units is this dose?

items.label: a day at four times a day

test.q: A baby is prescribed nystatin oral suspension 100,000 units four times a day for 7 days. The label reads 100,000 units in 1 mL. What total volume is needed for the course? Please use the correct unit.
test.why: Each dose = 100,000 ÷ 100,000 × 1 = 1 mL. Per day = 4 × 1 = 4 mL. Course = 4 × 7 = 28 mL.

whyNot.0: This is one day's volume, not the 7-day course.
whyNot.1: This counts one dose a day; the prescription is four times a day.
whyNot.2: This uses 10,000 units in 1 mL, a tenfold error.
